Create a boxplot of observed resolution hours by service and overlay the individual values. Label units and groups. Write one observation and one caution about interpreting groups with small or unequal observed counts.

title: Evidence starts with the data
text: Learn to ask useful statistical questions, inspect software data, and communicate conclusions with appropriate uncertainty. This course is designed for master’s students in Software Engineering who know basic Python and are new to statistics.

title: Evidence starts with the data
text:
Start here

Read the course syllabus.
Prepare Jupyter or Google Colab using the setup guide.
Open Session 1: Statistical questions and data.

Sessions 1–4 have complete learning packages. Sessions 5–10 are planned and do not yet have published materials. Each meeting lasts 90 minutes; the full course has 15 contact hours.

title: Evidence starts with the data
text:
Our recurring case
A software team wants to compare incident resolution across deployed versions. Before calculating a difference, we must understand what a record represents and whether the export can support that comparison. We use a small, openly licensed synthetic incident dataset to practice those decisions.

title: Evidence starts with the data
text:
Learning through practice
Every session combines concepts, a worked example, guided notebook practice, and a short formative assessment. Sessions 1–4 use criterion-based feedback; any course-grade weighting and final project policy will be announced separately. Bring your questions and explain your decisions in words as well as code.

title: Syllabus
text:
By the end of the full course, you will import, summarize, visualize, and analyze data with Python; connect statistical procedures to a study design; and communicate estimates, uncertainty, and limitations. Basic Python knowledge is assumed. Prior statistics knowledge is not required.
All 10 sessions are delivered live over videoconference; there are no in-person meetings. Join from the link shared before each session.

title: Session 4 · Exploratory visualization

During the session
Build an exploratory panel with a histogram of all observed durations, a boxplot with visible observations by service, and bars comparing incident records with observed durations. In a virtual breakout room, exchange one interpretation and one caution; revise the panel so another reader can identify the variables, units, and denominators without narration.
The shared data contain 24 fictional closed incidents and 21 observed resolution_hours values. This variable is opening-to-closure time in hours, not response latency. There is no meaningful date or second numerical measure in this dataset, so an incident identifier is not a time axis and a trend should not be invented.
